t: Posh Jewish Man and his Wife
x: A Posh Jewish Man and his wife were present at Jesus's speech in Monty Python's Life of Brian. He and his wife were crucified at the end of the film.
Picasso/Cycling Race is a sketch from "Whither Canada?," the first episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The "It's the Arts" linkman, David Mitzie (Michael Palin) introduces the segment where Pablo Picasso would be painting a picture whilst riding a bicycle. Baxter (Palin) then presents the route Picasso would be taking. Vicky (Eric Idle) tells the audience about the technical specifications of Picasso's bike and how well he will fare on the road.

Reg Moss (Idle) then reports that Picasso has yet to have been spotted, but interviews Mr Ron Geppo (Graham Chapman), British Cycling Sprint Champion, who predicts that Picasso will be fine as long as he does not attempt a too-sophisticated painting.

As Picasso has been reported to be approaching the Tolworth roundabout on the A3, Sam Trench (John Cleese) excitedly narrates as he reports seeing Picasso and describes the painting so far, but soon is told by a pepperpot (Palin) that it is actually Kandinsky, followed by Braque and Mondrian.

Then approaching are Chagall, Ernst, Miró, Dufy, Nicholson, Pollock, Buffet, Brâncuși, Géricault, Léger, Delaunay, de Kooning, Kokoschka, Paul Klee, and Schwitters. However, Trench reports no sign of Picasso.

Mitzie then reports that Picasso has fallen off of his bicycle and, as such, has failed in his first bid for international cycling fame. He then signs off (pushing a pig underneath his desk in the process).

A Sportsview-esque montage of artistic activities follows before a man says to "Hold it".
- "Saturday Sports" performed by the Bosworth Orchestra in 1951, from a BBC LP.

- This sketch was written by Michael Palin and Terry Jones.
- The links involving the viking were pre-recorded before the main studio recording to minimise costume changes.
- The scenes with Reg Moss and Sam Trench were filmed on Walton Road and Gaston Bridge Road respectively, both in Walton-on-Thames, on July 17th 1969.
- Assistant floor manager Roger Last appears as one of the cyclists.
- The Sportsview montage used footage from the BBC film library and shows Henry Moore and John Betjeman.
- After Vicky hands back to Mitzie, there was to be a scene where Mitzie hands back to Baxter, who says "Well, we'll be taking you back as soon as there's any more news of Picasso. In the meantime, some music", which was to lead into the Johann Gambolputty sketch, originally written and filmed for this episode. This sequence was deleted in the editing stage.
Police Raid is a sketch that appears in "Man's Crisis of Identity in the Latter Half of the 20th Century," the fifth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Two men (Eric Idle and John Cleese) play chess until Police Constable Henry Thatcher (Graham Chapman) interrupts to announce that he is raiding the establishment due to certain substances being in the vicinity. The first man, the actor Sandy Camp (Idle) repeatedly asks what sort of substances he is referring to, but Thatcher is intentionally vague and evasive each time. After several attempts at questioning, Thatcher warns Camp that outside he has a police dog, Josephine, who is trained to sniff out 'certain substances' but is also, he admits, a 'junkie'. This thoroughly confuses Camp who begins to grow fed up with Thatcher when, suddenly, he removes a paper bag from his pocket and plants it in the premises, intending to frame the two men. Camp calls him out on his ruse and examines the bag to find... sandwiches. Thatcher turns to the camera and comically wonders what he gave the wife.

In response to the sketch, E.B. Debenham (Mrs) (Carol Cleveland) writes a letter in defence of her husband, who, like a lot of people his age, is fifty.

Brigadier Arthur Gormanstrop (Mrs) writes a response to the previous letter, offended, as he is nearly sixty, and is quite mad.

Various people, including a pepperpot, are interviewed about satire.

- This sketch was written by Michael Palin and Terry Jones.
- Thatcher's line about what he might have given the wife was originally scheduled to end with the wife (Palin), obviously inebriated, saying "I don't know, baby, but it's better than lunch" while flinging eggs across the kitchen with a frying pan, as if it were a tennis racket. This scene was recorded but cut before transmission, at the insistence of the BBC. No known copies exist of the sketch with this line included.
- The aforementioned deleted scene of Thatcher's wife was pre-recorded before the main studio recording.
- The sketch is a satire of British police officer Norman Pilcher, who became infamous in the 1960s for arresting a number of celebrities on drug charges, and was widely suspected of planting evidence. His police career ended in disgrace in 1972 and was imprisoned for perjury.
Police station is a sketch that appears in "You're No Fun Anymore," the seventh episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A police spokesperson (Graham Chapman) reads The Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire by Googie Withers, then interrupts the science fiction story and says that Angus Podgorny could have saved his wife's life in the previous sketch by going to the police. A knight approaches him, prepared to hit him in the head with a chicken.

Podgorny (Michael Palin) speaks to a detective (Eric Idle) about the blancmange eating his wife. The detective blames the crime on Jack Riley, blancmange impersonator and cannibal. The blancmange shows up and eats the detective, who realises that it is not Riley, but an extraterrestrial being.
- Terry Jones was originally to play the girl at the police station.
Pet Conversations is a sketch that appears in "Untitled," the tenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

At a Pet Shop somewhere near Melton Mowbray, a man (John Cleese) enters to buy a cat, but the shopkeeper (Michael Palin) insists on selling him a terrier, even offering to physically alter it in order to look like a cat. The man changes his mind to wanting to buy a parrot, but the shopkeeper continues to insist on the terrier, offering to convert it into a parrot. Because the parrot conversion would not be finished by the time the man needs the parrot, the shopkeeper offers to convert it into a fish instead. The man accepts, on the condition that he can watch the conversion.

Two men (John Cleese, Eric Idle) comment on this being "predictable" and "done before," a Centurion (Terry Jones) adding that they did it for Caesar's Christmas show. Caesar (Graham Chapman) then corrects the Centurion, saying they did Jack and the Beanstalk.

- This sketch was originally submitted for inclusion in the BBC's annual Christmas Night with the Stars show, in November 1969. The sketch was rejected for its content and Confuse-a-Cat was featured instead. The sketch was later filmed as part of "Untitled" in December 1969.
Quiz Programme: "Wishes" is a sketch that appears in "Intermission," the thirteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

An interviewer (John Cleese) interviews two small boys (Eric Idle and Michael Palin). He asks Eric if he wants a 16-ton weight dropped on top of him, to which he responds "Don't know." He asks the other boy what he wants, and he says he wants to have Raquel Welch dropped on top of him.

He then interviews Trevor Atkinson (Graham Chapman) who says he is 42. He also interviews his friend, (Michael Palin) who talks about his insurance job. The interviewer asks Trevor what his big wish would be, and Trevor responds "more fairy stories about the police." A fairy godmother (Idle) hops into shot and says "And so you shall" before waving her wand.

It cuts to a policeman (Terry Jones) who gets off his bike, takes out a burglar costume and pumps it up. The burglar then runs away and the policeman summons three other policemen and they follow the burglar through the countryside. The burglar then catches them in a huge gift box and runs off, before the fairy godmother dressed as a policeman makes him disappear.

Another policeman (Palin) tells the audience the Special Crime Squad have been using wands for a year now, and how easy they are to use. Something the truncheons can't do.
Probe-Around on Crime is a sketch that appears in "Intermission," the thirteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

'Panorama' music plays whilst photos of policemen posing in tutus is shown under text saying 'Probearound'. The presenter (John Cleese) introduces the topic of crime, only to be shot dead.

A man (Eric Idle) walks into scene, apologizing for the shooting, but states that he always introduces the programme, not the dead presenter and kicks the cadaver off the desk. He takes the spot before rhetorically asking, "What are the police up to?" before a cut to a policeman (Terry Jones) who is up to page 39 in a book.

The presenter then introduces Harry H. "Snapper" Organs (Michael Palin) who is sitting next to a Viking. Inspector Organs, while pinning needles on a voodoo doll, is encouraging magic in the police force. The Ex-King Zog of Albania calls in, but the presenter cancels the call. The presenter asks what kind of magic is being introduced, before cutting to a scene of four policemen moving a tumbler around an Ouija board and they spell out 'UP YOURS', surprising them for its insult at them. It then cuts to another policeman who taps his wand on cars parked in 'No Parking' areas to make them disappear. Another policeman standing in the middle of a road transports an old woman across the road with a flick of his magic wand. Then, five policeman zooms past the camera on broomsticks.
Psychiatry is a sketch that appears in "Intermission," the thirteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Dr Larch (John Cleese) sits in his office before the nurse (Carol Cleveland) comes in to tell him that Mr Phelps had arrived before Larch tells her to make it clear that he's a psychiatrist, but she tells him he'll have to do it himself. Phelps (Terry Jones) enters dressed as Napoleon and criticises Dr Larch for being predictable, and leaves without doing his first line. A man in the corridor announces "Albatross!" and Larch tells him to shut up before being irritated, stating it drives him mad. It cuts to a man (Michael Palin) who remarks "a mad psychiatrist, that would be new."

It cuts back to Larch who welcomes the man, Mr Notlob (Palin), into his office by phrasing different subjects which Mr Notlob proclaims Dr Larch is a mad psychiatrist, but he says he is not, resulting a cut to Mr Phelps, blowing a raspberry before cutting back to Larch, who asks Mr Notlob what his problem is. Mr Notlob says he keeps hearing guitars playing and people singing when there's no one around. During his diagnosis, the two hear 'We're All Going to the Zoo Tomorrow', and Notlob explains it's usually folk songs, as he heard 'We'll Never Fall in Love Again' for six hours last night. Larch tells him to see a specialist who has an office like this one.
Photos of Uncle Ted is a sketch that appears in "The Spanish Inquisition," the fifteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

An old lady (Marjorie Wilde) shows a young lady (Carol Cleveland) pictures of the man in the previous sketch who says he would tax holiday snaps. She shows her pictures of Uncle Ted standing in various positions around a house, with the young lady ripping every photo that is handed to her, bored. Just then, she shows her a picture of the Spanish Inquisition hiding behind the coal shed, and the young lady exclaims "I didn't expect the Spanish Inquisition!".
Race Against the Credits is a sketch that appears in "The Spanish Inquisition," the fifteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

After failing to turn up to the courtroom in the previous sketch in time, the Cardinals rush out of a suburban house and onto a red bus, climbing to the top deck. Biggles (Terry Jones) notices the credits have started to roll and Ximinez (Michael Palin) tells the ticket man to hurry. Ximinez notices the lighting credits and then the producer credits have appeared and they must hurry. The Cardinals race into the building, jump into the courtroom and Ximinez announces "Nobody expects the Span-" before being cut off by 'THE END'.
- Ximinez's "Oh bugger!" was a point of contention for the BBC but they soon decided to let it pass uncut. It was censored for viewers in Scotland though.
Psychiatrist Milkman is a sketch that appears in "Déjà Vu," the sixteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Mrs Pim (Graham Chapman) sits in the living room knitting, before the doorbell rings and she goes to answer it. A man in a milkman's uniform (Eric Idle) introduces himself as a psychiatrist, and the lady points this out, to which the psychiatrist ticks off on his notebook. The lady tells him to go away but the milkman proceeds. He continues to test her and concludes she suffers from repressive libido complex with multiple reasons, such as an unhappy childhood. The psychiatrist tells her to come down to the dairy as it won't cure her but will give hundreds of workers a good laugh, and she agrees.

The psychiatrist leads her out of her home, past a cat which explodes, into his milk van filled with folders of case histories, and drives off. The doctor (Michael Palin) flags down the milk van and tells him their psychiatrist from Jersey Cream Psychiatrists hasn't arrived yet. The psychiatrist begins to treat him and recognises him from the last sketch. He tells the doctor he suffers from severe personality disorder.
Poets is a sketch that appears in "The Buzz Aldrin Show," the seventeenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A sales manager of the East Midlands Poet Board (John Cleese) tells the audience that a poet is essential for home comfort and all-year-round reliability. They hope to have a poet in every home by the end of next year. It cuts to an advertisement with a song about their service.

A woman (Terry Jones) answers her front door where an inspector (Michael Palin) has come to 'read her poet'. She directs him to the cupboard under the stairs where William Wordsworth (Eric Idle) reads I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud. The Inspector looks around the cupboard and starts to leave but the woman tries to engage in conversation. She remarks about the weather and the inspector launches into a full weather forecast, pulling down a map of the UK.

A BBC continuity announcer (Idle) announces choice of viewing on BBC 1 or 2.

The woman switches the TV off and pours the inspector a cup of tea, asking about his job. He starts to leave but the woman compliments his torch. The woman tries to keep the inspector from leaving and asks him to look at her Thomas Hardy in the bedroom. She launches herself onto him and asks his name, Wombat Harness, who hastily agrees to look at her Thomas Hardy.
Police Constable Pan-Am is a sketch that appears in "The Buzz Aldrin Show," the seventeenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Police Constable Pan-Am  (Graham Chapman) refuses to listen to anyone and unrightfully insults the chemist in the previous sketch. When the customer (Eric Idle) points to the shoplifter (Terry Gilliam) but the policeman arrests him and makes aeroplane noises. The shoplifter denies and his friend (Stanley Mason) pokes his head out from under his coat and says he's a witness.

The policeman tells the chemist he'll "do him for heresy" and the chemist exclaims "Heresy? Blimey, I didn't expect the Spanish Inquisition" but the policeman shuts him up, takes a product, and tells him he's taking him down to the police station.

The policeman then calls Buzz Aldrin and makes funny noises and singing, arresting the customer. A BBC voiceover (John Cleese) apologises to the police regarding the character of Police Constable Pan-Am.

A picture of Buzz Aldrin appears on screen and the credits run as The Star Spangled Banner plays.
Poofy Judges is a sketch that appears in "Archaeology Today," the twenty-first episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus. It also appears in Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl.

Two judges (Eric Idle and Michael Palin) walk along a chamber with justly music playing. They walk into a changing room and converse in camp manners, undressing their wigs and robes, commenting on their day's work. They reveal sparkly, erotic playsuits under their robes.
Puss in Boots is a sketch from "Mr and Mrs Brian Norris' Ford Popular", the twenty-eighth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The ship crew are brought in, this time without trousers. The officer (Terry Gilliam), also without trousers, tells his captain (John Cleese) that he found them walking on the beach, to which the ship's captain (Terry Jones) tells him they are British Naval officers before a woman (Julia Breck) comes in, dressed a principal boy, holding a stuffed cat and proclaimed Puss in Boots, to which the police captain tells them to stop as they are in the 'Police Department of the State of Venezuela', before she starts a small talk along saying 'Oh, no, it isn't' as the naval officers also join in before the police captain gets out a gun and shuts them up while coming from behind his desk, also not wearing trousers. He asks the naval officers what ship they're from to which the captain tells a story about the 'SS Mothergoose', during which the officer (Eric Idle), who also isn't wearing trousers, tells the captain he got 30 bob for the trousers.

As the naval captain tells his story, stagehands take the set apart, revealing that they are in a living room until Mrs. Kelly (Michael Palin) and her husband (Graham Chapman) come in, demanding why they're doing Horse of the Year in the living room, told by Mr. Fox. The police captain actor tells her they had the wrong room as they're BBC 2 before the naval captain actor tells her that BBC 1 are in the kitchen. Concerned about her binette, they take off with Mr. Kelly telling them to turn the gas off before they leave as the actors continue their play. In the hallway outside the kitchen, the Kellys hear Harvey Smith crash, forcing Mrs. Kelly to kick the entire BBC group out of her house, including Mr. Fox (Jones) and the presenter (Idle).

The credits are names written on sheets of scattered paper on the Kelly's floor.
- Puss in Boots is the same name of a Shrek character. In fact, John Cleese starred in the three Shrek movies.
Programme Titles Conference is a sketch that appears in "The Light Entertainment War," the forty-second episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The BBC Chief Executive (Terry Jones) watches Mrs Elizabeth III (Jones) as she dances about in the car park, proclaiming that the public are idiots, even wondering if they should show the last 5 miles of the M2 so that they can tune in to the BBC. He then tells a group of planners (Eric Idle, Michael Palin, Graham Chapman and an uncredited actor) they ought show the last five miles of the M2 since the public is so stupid. The first planner (Idle), says the M2 repeat has given them 97,300,912 views and ITV nought, and give B roads their own series, but the executive rejects it. The second planner (Palin) thinks they're talking about budgies while the third planner (Chapman) think they're talking about cake when the executive mentions it. The first planner then mentions repeating and they assume it was either reheating or repeating cakes before the planner tells them it is time for a break, only to realise he was looking at the clock wrong.

The first planner then suggests they retitle the repeats, which the executive approves. The second planner suggests ‘Dad’s Navy’, the first suggests ‘Up Your Mother Next Door’, and the third suggests (off topic) ‘Doctor At Bee’, confusing them. Someone soon knocks at the door and the first planner tells them, but the executive thinks he was suggesting ‘Someone's Knocking At the Door’ as a title, which is too long. The second planner then suggests ‘I Married Lucy’, even though it has already been done. The third planner (off topic again) suggests ‘Doctor At Three’, confusing the executive. When there was a knock at the door again, the first planner informs them, but the executive, again, thinks he's passing it as a title, ‘I Think Someone's Knocking At the Door’, which is even longer. The second planner then suggests ‘I Married a Tree’, the executive suggests ‘And Mother Makes Tree’, the third planner (once again, off topic) suggests ‘Doctor At Cake’.

After another knock at the door, the first planner tells them, but the executive again thinks he is passing it off as a title ‘Look! I'm Not Absolutely Certain, But, Well I Do Rather Get the Impression That There is Someone Actually Knocking on the Door At This Very Moment’, and tells him to stop lengthening it. The third planner (fourth time off topic) suggests ‘I Married a Cake’, the second suggests ‘I Married Three Rabbit Jelly Moulds’ before the person behind the door (Terry Gilliam) loudly tells them to open the door. The executive believes ‘Open the Sodding Door’ is a title suggestion, and rejects it, not wanting to use ‘sodding’. The door soon opens, revealing the person, a security guard in a wheelchair and a sword through his head, who comes in, and they tell him off for not knocking. The guard tries to tell them there is trouble in Studio 5, but they believe he is suggesting titles before he turns on a nearby TV to show the Courtmartial/Basingstoke in Westphalia sketch as the third planner was about to, only to nudge the guard, who yells in pain, shouting ‘Mind me war wound!’, which they approve the title ‘Mind Me War Wound’.
Philip Jenkinson on Cheese Westerns is a sketch that appears in "Salad Days," the thirty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

It is revealed the Cheese Shop sketch is a preview of the first 'cheese Western' called Rogue Cheddar, with later cheese Westerns being Gunfight and Gruyère Corral, Ilchester '73 and The Cheese Who Shot Libery Valance. Philip Jenkinson (Eric Idle) transitions to talking about one of his favourite directors, Sam Peckinpah. Captions appear at the bottom of the screen 'GET ON WITH IT', 'AND STOP SNIFFING' and 'WILL YOU STOP SNIFFING'. He introduces 'Salad Days'.
Prices on the Planet Algon is a sketch that appears in "The Nude Organist," the thirty-fifth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A voiceover (John Cleese) introduces the planet Algon, where the price for a cup of drinking chocolate costs £4 million, and an immersion heater costs over £6 billion, and split-crotch panties would be unattainable. He continues presenting the ridiculous prices of ordinary objects.

A presenter James M'Burke (Michael Palin) gets news on the relative inexpensiveness of a mower, and how Algon may be a good planet for those with large gardens, before passing over to another presenter to present Live pictures from Algon. The presenter, Harry (Terry Jones), cites the lack of shops but can't see much. James asks whether the split-crotch panties will be exclusively unattainable on Algon. Professor Herman Khan, a scientist notorious for finding lingerie on planets that can't sustain life, (Eric Idle) answers that question - they might be found on other parts of the planet.

More live pictures come through, showing a bird (or a woman (Lyn Ashley)) hopping through the Algon landscape. The live feed cuts, to the scientists' disappointment.

Mr. Badger (Idle) appears, explaining the BBC have let him read the credits for 40p. He reads out the credits as the theme music plays. Once he's finished, a 16-ton weight falls on him.
Pornographic Bookshop is a sketch that appears in "E. Henry Thripshaw's Disease," the thirty-sixth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The bookshop assistant (Eric Idle) is showing a customer (John Cleese) all the porn on sale. The customer enquires on books about English architecture, but eventually settles on Lord Lieutenant in Nylon. The previous shop assistant (Terry Jones) yells his Tudor jargon and the wall slides open. Superintendent Gaskell (Michael Palin) enters and announces this is a raid. The shop assistant is sure he's still acting undercover, convinced he's Sir Philip Sidney, and continues to sell porn to a customer (Terry Gilliam). Gaskell's companion Maddox is missing so he promises the shopkeeper it's a raid, trying to prove he's a policeman.

All the customers leave through a door, and Gaskell follows them through to a Tudor garden. He comes across a Tudor woman called Frances (Rosalind Bailey) who weeps in his arms how her love has gone. Her father walks over and recognises him as Sir Philip Sidney and invites him to dinner, to which he accepts.
Prejudice is a sketch that appears in "Dennis Moore," the thirty-seventh episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The over-excited host (Michael Palin) presents the gameshow 'Prejudice', where you can have a go at insulting all types of ethnicities. The first question comes from a lady who is going on a cruise in the Mediterranean and can't find anything wrong with the Syrians. The host answers that they are dirty, smelly and untrustworthy, hoping to help with her problem.

He moves on to last week's competition of finding a derogatory term for Belgians, choosing the runner-ups: "the Sprouts", "the Phlegms", and the winner: "miserable fat Belgian bastards". The next item on the show is "Shoot the Poof". As the first contestant goes on stage, he's shot by a camp highwayman (Palin) who in turn is shot by Dennis Moore (John Cleese), who stops a coach in its path. He orders them to take out their valuables. Then he inspects it and redistributes it so he and everyone else has the same amount.

After the credits, a judge (Palin) from the Ideal Loon Exhibition is riding the bus home with his companion (Terry Jones) who reassures him he should've won. Behind them, another judge (Graham Chapman) is sobbing and his wife (Eric Idle) scolds him. The bus with 'The End' as the destination drives away.

Pontius Pilate is the main antagonist of the Monty Python film, Monty Python's Life of Brian. He was played by Michael Palin. He was the fifth governor of the Roman Empire in Judea and also had rhotacism, making it when he says "Roman" it would sound like "woman". He is friends with Julius Caesar, but was best friends with a soldier by the name of Biggus Dickus, and his wife Incontinentia Buttocks. He and Nisus Wettus are the ones who send criminals to crucifixion, such as Brian, Jesus and Mr. Cheeky. He has a tense relationship with the Centurion, who often misunderstands his speech and tries unsuccessfully to shield him from public embarrassment.
Penguins/BBC Programme Planners is a sketch that appears in "A Book at Bedtime," the thirty-eighth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A presenter (John Cleese) introduces the idea that penguins may actually help scientists "fathom the uncharted depths of the human mind". Professor Ken Rosewall (Graham Chapman) presents his theory that the penguin is more intelligent than the human being, with such proof as the penguin's brain is smaller than a human's and therefore will still be smaller even if the penguin is the size of a human. Another scientist Peaches Bartkowicz (Michael Palin) theorises that the penguin would have to be 66 feet tall to have the same brain size as a human, and walks over to a giant penguin.

Professor Rosewall calls this the 'Waste of time theory' but presents more evidence, including the fact that in IQ tests, penguins scored worse than primitive human subgroups, but better than BBC programme planners. However, Rosewall suggests one particularly dim programme planner may have lowered the average score, and the screen cuts to black with the words 'you can say that again'.

Dr Lewis Hoad (Eric Idle) explains the unfairness that the penguins aren't educated. The scene cuts to another scientist reading questions to penguins in their own environment - in a zoo enclosure. The problem of the environment barrier has been solved, but not the language barrier. Therefore, the next experiment is asking penguins and a group of non-English-speaking humans the same questions in the same environment. To no one's surprise, the humans and penguins score equally, and using this study, the BBC has decided to replace their higher-execs with penguins. Animations shows penguins taking over positions of power around the world.

Prof. F.H. Gumby is a Gumby. He liked to hoard history books about the Battle of Trafalgar. He thought that we should reappraise our concept of Trafalgar, which he got from R.J. Gumby and his friend being asked the controversy of Trafalgar by R.J. Canning. He was played by Eric Idle.

"Well, Well!" - L.R. Gumby screaming

Prof. L.R. Gumby was a Gumby professor and historian. He was played by Graham Chapman and is normally seen by windows screaming and yelling even if he doesn't have to like when he yelled at Prof. F.H. Gumby even though he agreed with him, in the R.J. Gumby, His Friend and Professor Canning Battle of Trafalgar argument.

Prof. Enid Gumby is a Gumby. He likes to hang out in pig pens and look at them from time to time. When Prof. F.H. and Prof. L.R. started agreeing to each other's Trafalgar theory that R.J. and his Friend made, he said that cement is more interesting than people think. He was played by John Cleese.

Prince Herbert is a character in Monty Python and the Holy Grail, the heir apparent of Swamp Castle, played by Terry Jones. His father, the swamp king, arranges for him to marry Princess Lucky, whose father is one of the biggest landowners in Britain. However Herbert is uninterested in land and wishes to marry a woman for love instead. He is always trying to express his feelings in song, to the king's annoyance.

The king imprisons him in the castle tower under the supervision of two dim-witted guards. He shoots an arrow with a note from the tower that leads to his near-rescue by Sir Lancelot, who is embarrassed to discover that the damsel he set out to free is a boy. As Lancelot explains himself to the king, Herbert dangles from the window on a cord of knotted bedsheets still hoping to escape. The king casually cuts the cord and presumes the prince dead, but he turns out to have survived and sings his story to the wedding guests.

The Performing Minstrels were a group of singing minstrels who would do shows and songs for King Arthur and his knights. They first appeared during the Camelot Song and reappeared as Robin's favourites. During the quest, Robin went up into the mountains and listened to his minstrel's song until it started to get disturbing. Then he met a Three-Headed Giant and when he ran away the minstrels made fun of him. They were eaten by the knights during winter.
Poetry Reading (Ants) is a sketch that appears in "Michael Ellis," the forty-first episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

In a Victorian-style room, an old lady (Graham Chapman) is hosting a poets gathering, with William Wordsworth (Terry Jones), Percy Bysshe Shelley (Terry Gilliam), John Keats (Eric Idle) and Alfred Lord Tennyson (John Hughman) among the attendees. First she says their names wrong and then invites "Wandworth" to read his poem "I Wandered Lonely as a Crab". Wordsworth reads his well-known poem, with a reference to ants in the end. The lady invites Shelley to read his poem "Ode to a Crab" by Shelley stands up and announces it's actually called "Ozymandias", and begins to read, causing the audience to erupt into applause from all the ant references he inserted.

The lady, tipsy from the sherry she's been drinking, invites Keats to read "Ode to a Glass of Sherry". He begins to aggressively read a poem of a frightening anteater, with the audience protesting loudly in horror. The lady pushes Keats out the room, and asks Tennyson to read his poem "The Charge of the Ant Brigade". As he begins to read, Queen Victoria (Michael Palin) enters to a fanfare, with Prince Albert being carried in a coffin. She begins to address the problem of ants reoccurring in today's poetry, failing to hide her German accent. She asks them to write about nicer things and leaves, with Chris Quinn (Idle) sneaking out, having watched the whole meeting from the back of the crowd.
RAF Banter is a sketch that appears in "The Light Entertainment War," the forty-second episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Squadron leader (Eric Idle) and Squiffy (Terry Jones) greet each other and Squadron leader tells a story of RAF banter in thick RAF slang. Squiffy asks Wingco (Graham Chapman) to help him out understanding the banter, and Squadron leader retells the story but he doesn't understand either. An air raid siren sounds and another pilot (Michael Palin) enters spurting out RAF slang. The other three men are confused, and tell him they don't understand his banter. A narrator (Idle) says how cabbage crates were dropped on London.
Pig is a sketch that appears in "Whither Canada?," the first episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A chalk pig runs out of the other sketches’ chalkboard (because it's afraid it might be crossed out as well) and gets eaten by a man sporting a mustache, glasses, and a suit with a tie. A big hand takes the man's head off and breaks it like an egg. The yolk from within the egg falls into a bowl and onto another man's head.
Police Helmets is a sketch that appears in "Hamlet," the forty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The policeman (Michael Palin) asks John Dull (Graham Chapman) what he's wearing on his head. John answers 'a helmet', and the policeman points out the number on his helmet, proving it is an authentic Metropolitan Area policeman helmet. He then crosses the road, stopping the traffic and slaps Mrs Edgeworth, takes her armchair and sits down next to John, telling him more about his authentic policeman helmet.

He starts talking about the Tsar's private army's helmets and looks for some paper to draw it on, stealing some out of a passer-by's briefcase. He nicks another's pen, and draws the shape of the helmet. He spots two ladies sitting on a bench and asks John if he'd like some lunch. He goes up to them, takes their lunch for forensic examination because it might have been used as a murder weapon, and joins back with John. He leaves again to get some beer, smashing glass and setting off an alarm offscreen, and sits back down with two bottles of beer. As he begins to talk about helmets more, the camera pans away to a couple across the street, making out on the pavement.
Piston Engine is a sketch that appears in "Hamlet," the forty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Mrs Robinson and Mrs Non-Robinson have a conversation. Mrs Robinson has bought a piston engine. A woman sitting on a park bench (Eric Idle) listening to The Robinsons chucks the radio away saying it's rubbish, and the doctor in the hospital ward (Graham Chapman) says he wanted to listen to that.

Mrs Gorilla (Michael Palin) joins Mrs Non-Gorilla (Idle) at the park bench, and the two repeat the conversation heard on the radio. Mrs Non-Gorilla shows her the piston engine she bought and the camera pans away to Mrs Non-Smoker (Terry Jones) who is throwing her shopping at birds. Mrs Smoker (Graham Chapman) joins her, and they repeat the conversation on the radio. Mrs Smoker has bought a piston engine, and Mrs Non-Smoker buys it off her for £3. They begin to recite Hamlet lines.
Queen Victoria Handicap is a sketch that appears in "Hamlet," the forty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A commentator Peter (Eric Idle) commentates a race between Queen Victorias as they run around the racetrack and jump over hedges.

The 'A Room in Polonius's House' presenter Frank Bough (Michael Palin), dressed as Queen Victoria, thanks Peter for his commentary and announces that Real Madrid striker Miguel Otana was sent off for breaking wind in the 43rd minute. He hands over to Brian Clough (Idle), also dressed as Queen Victoria, who shares his opinion over footage of the football match. The presenter then turns to Jimmy Hill, also dressed as Queen Victoria, who reports on the ridiculous reasons that referees send players off for. The presenter then turns to Hamlet (Terry Jones) and starts talking about the girl on the bed with her legs up against the mantelpiece before a nurse (Carol Cleveland) ushers him out.

A title card 'Act Five - A Ham In The Castle' is shown on screen, and a production of Hamlet is performed by a cast of Queen Victorias. They gather for the final applause as the credits roll.

After, a ragged man (Palin) emerges from an explosion in an empty field and says "And then..."
Post Box Ceremony is a sketch that appears in "Mr Neutron," the forty-fourth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A man rides through a suburban street on a horse-drawn carriage calling for iron, and housewives put air missiles in it.

A mayor and a GPO official (Michael Palin) join some civilians on a rostrum and the official begins the opening ceremony of a new post box on Ulveston Road, talking about the benefits to the community this box will have. He then repeats himself in French, and German.
Pepperpots Discuss French Philosophers is a sketch that appears in "Sex and Violence," the second episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Four Pepperpots (Graham Chapman, Terry Jones, Michael Palin and John Cleese) are interviewed about French people. They come to the conclusion that they think well, bringing up Pascal, Sartre, Voltaire and Descartes.

- This sketch was filmed at FJ Wallis at Unit 9 of the Shopping Precinct on Acton High Street, on July 14th 1969.
- This sketch was originally longer. Rousseau and Kierkegaard were also mentioned before the latter was found out to be Danish, to which the Pepperpots expressed their disdain. They then continued to express their disdain for German philosophers, naming Kant, Nietzsche and Von Leibnitz. They were asked if they would swap a French philosopher (Descartes) for two German philosophers (Hegel and Heidegger) to which they declined, saying "We'll keep the Descartes". The sketch was trimmed in the editing stages, however, for timing reasons, although the cut section can be found as a bonus feature on Network's Blu-Ray release of Monty Python's Flying Circus.
Sam Peckinpah's "Salad Days" is a sketch that appears in "Salad Days," the thirty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

In a fine example of the Python team's fondness of the 'double spoof', this third series sketch targets both the genteel stage musical Salad Days and the work of the controversial American film director Sam Peckinpah.

Well-dressed, well-spoken, upper-class youngsters frolic in an idyllic garden around an upright piano, responding enthusiastically to a man named Lionel's (Michael Palin) suggestion of a game of tennis. Things go awry when Lionel is struck in the face by the ball, causing blood to seep through his fingers. He reflexively flings his racquet towards the stomach of a girl, impaling her before she soon faints, tearing another man's (Eric Idle) arm off in the process. The man staggers across to the piano and slams down the lid, severing both of the pianist's (John Cleese) hands. The piano then collapses in slow motion, crushing some screaming women to death. Another man (Graham Chapman) gets impaled by the piano keyboard, which slices off a woman's head when he turns around, with other people acting like nothing ever happened.

It soon cuts back to the studio, prompting Philip Jenkinson (Idle) to smugly remark "Pretty strong meat there from [sniff] Sam Peckinpah!" before he is gunned down in slow motion, with much spurting blood (and the caption "Tee Hee").

The end credits roll over his dying agonies, before a serious-sounding voiceover (Cleese) reads an apology to everyone in the entire world, which is then denied by a frivolous-sounding voiceover (Idle).

- Robert Hewison's book, Monty Python - The Case Against, contains extracts from a BBC viewer's panel's response to the show, and naturally there were complaints that this particular sketch was "over the top", "horrific", and "sick".

Self-Defence (also known as Self-Defence Against Fresh Fruit) is a sketch that appears in "Owl Stretching Time," the fourth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus. It also appears in And Now for Something Completely Different.

The teacher (John Cleese) is about to start off his class, but he notices that everyone, save for four students, is absent. He starts off the class by carrying on from where they got to last week, when he was showing them how to defend themselves against anyone who attacks with a piece of fresh fruit. The class complains that for the last nine weeks, all he's been teaching them is fruit. One student (Eric Idle) keeps on insisting that they should be taught how to defend themselves against anyone who attacks with a pointed stick. The teacher yells at the student for thinking that pointed sticks are more dangerous than fresh fruit.

He starts off the class with passionfruit, but the whole class complains that they've done passionfruit, as well as oranges, apples, grapefruit (whole and segmented), pomegranates, greengages, grapes, lemons, plums, mangoes in syrup, and cherries (red and black). The teacher decides to teach them about bananas. He tells them, to defend themselves against a man armed with a banana, first, he has to be forced to drop the banana, then the banana has to be eaten, thus disarming him and rendering him helpless. When another student (Michael Palin) asks about a man armed with a bunch of bananas, the teacher tells him to shut up. The student from before again chimes in to ask about a man with a pointed stick, to which the teacher also tells him to shut up. He demonstrates by asking a student called Mr Harrison (Graham Chapman) (whom the teacher calls Mr Apricot), to attack him with a banana, but just as Harrison is about to attack him, the teacher shoots him dead, and eats the banana. The movie version ends here.

Continuing the TV sketch, a student named Thompson (Terry Jones) mentions a pineapple, the one thing the teacher seems afriad of. Then the teacher calls Thompson, to attack him with a raspberry, but Thompson refuses, saying that the teacher will shoot him. The teacher throws away the gun, and Thompson is about to attack him, when a 16-ton weight comes down on him. He then asks the remaining students to do the same, but they refuse until he promises not to kill them. As the students advance with baskets of raspberries, the teacher releases a tiger which attacks the remaining students. The teacher warns imaginary other students that he has wired himself up to 200 tons of gelignite, and blows himself up.

- In the draft script for the episode, this sketch led on from Hermits and ended the episode. Afterward, the Colonel would enter and ask "Where's the man who's been infringing the copyright of the army slogan" before a sudden explosion.
- The sketch may have inspired the creation of the Order of the Pineapple.

Raymond Luxury Yacht (pronounced ‘Throatwobbler Mangrove’) is a fictional character from the TV show Monty Python's Flying Circus, portrayed by Graham Chapman. Raymond appears in the second series episodes "It's a Living" and "How to Recognise Different Parts of the Body". He is best remembered for his extremely large polystyrene nose.

In his first appearance, in the episode "It's A Living", Raymond is the guest in a talk show hosted by Michael Palin. He is presented as "one of England's leading skin-specialists", but when the interviewer refers to him by his name, he proudly proclaims that his name "is spelt Raymond Luxury-Yacht, but it's pronounced Throatwobbler Mangrove" (possibly a reference to the Mangrove Warbler). Following this the interviewer tells Raymond that he won't continue the interview, because he thinks that Raymond is a "very silly person". Raymond accuses the interviewer of anti-semitism (as a reference to the stereotypical image of the large nosed-Jew), but the interviewer defends himself by pulling off Raymond's nose and pointing out that is made of plastic. Raymond's intentions are made clear when he says "I want to be on television!", to which the interviewer answers "You can't", and tells him that he can collect his nose at the reception.

Raymond next appears in "How to Recognise Different Parts of the Body", where his large plastic nose (as a distinct part of the body) is the reason for his return. This time he enters the office of a cosmetic surgeon, played by John Cleese. Raymond tells the surgeon, a little embarrassed, that he wants some plastic surgery performed on him. After some discussion it becomes clear that he's not satisfied with his large nose, which the surgeon refers to as "a startler". When the surgeon examines the nose he realizes that it's a fake. Raymond says that he'd still like the operation, to which the surgeon responds "You've already had the operation, you strange person". Raymond desperately asks for the operation, and the surgeon accepts on one condition - that they will go on a camping-holiday together. Upon hearing this Raymond looks straight into the camera, and cries happily "He asked me! He asked me!". The next shot shows Raymond and the surgeon jumping around in a forest, in slow-motion, holding hands.
- Although the name might be a reference to the Mangrove Warbler, his name is spelt 'Throatwobbler' in official sources.

Roger the Shrubber is a character in the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, portrayed by Eric Idle. He was a man who arranged, designed and sold shrubberies. When King Arthur and Sir Bedevere encountered the dreaded Knights who say Ni, they were tasked to find a shrubbery. Arriving at a nearby town, they demanded an old woman to tell them where they could buy a shrubbery. When she refused, they said "Ni!" several times to her. Roger rode up disapprovingly, then introduced himself as a shrubber. Bedevere absentmindedly started saying "Ni!" to him but King Arthur held him back and purchased one of Roger's shrubberies for the knights.

Reg Moss reports on the status of Pablo Picasso, who was due to be passing through whilst riding a bicycle and painting. Moss interviews Mr Ron Geppo.

Sam Trench is a reporter who excitedly narrates as he believes to see Pablo Picasso approaching, but soon finds himself narrating a race between Kandinsky, Braque, Mondrian, Chagall, Ernst, Miró, Dufy, Nicholson, Pollock, Buffet, Brâncuși, Géricault, Léger, Delaunay, de Kooning, Kokoschka, Paul Klee, and Schwitters. However, Trench reports no sign of Picasso.

Following the laughter deaths of Ernest Scribbler and his mother, Scotland Yard's crack inspector is sent into the Scribbler home to remove the deadly joke whilst somber music plays on gramophone records, aided by the men of Q division. However, these precautions do not save the inspector from fatality by sudden, violent comedy. He is portrayed by Graham Chapman.

Seduced Milkman is a sketch that appears in "How to Recognise Different Types of Trees From Quite a Long Way Away," the third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus. It also appears in And Now for Something Completely Different.

A milkman (Michael Palin) delivers milk to a house and the resident, a seductive woman (Thelma Taylor) urges him to come inside. He follows her upstairs and is ushered into a room with the door being locked behind him. Inside are several other milkmen (one dead) who have been in the room for a long time.

In the film version, the woman is played by Carol Cleveland.
- "Charmaine", performed by Mantovani and His Orchestra, from the 1955 LP "An Album in Waltz Time"

- This sketch was filmed on July 16th 1969 on Ullswater Road, Barnes.
- Only appearance of Thelma Taylor in the series.
- The bit may have been a dig at Benny Hill, who had only recently left the BBC for Thames Television - and, early in his life, worked as a milkman.
Secret Service Dentists is a sketch that appears in "Owl-Stretching Time," the fourth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Arthur Lemming (Eric Idle) goes to a bookstore to buy a book, but the nervous bookseller, Stapleton (John Cleese), insists that he has no books for sale and tries to dismiss him until Lemming says he was told to come there.

The bookseller tries to speak in code, which is lost on Lemming, who then supposes that something is going on, which the bookseller and another man with a gun (Dick Vosburgh) insist is untrue. When Lemming asks for a copy of An Illustrated History of False Teeth, the bookseller pulls a gun, asking how much he knows and accuses him of being from the British Dental Association, to which he says he is just a tobacconist.

An armed Lafarge (Michael Palin) enters and has Stapleton drop the gun and interrogates him on the location of the fillings. This goes on until the man, identified as Van Der Berg enters with a nurse (Carol Cleveland), who takes Stapleton and Lafarge's guns, and holds them both up, revealing he is not on either side. He then demands the fillings' location.

Brian (Terry Jones) then enters with a bazooka and holds them all up and demands to know where the fillings are until the Big Cheese (Graham Chapman) enters and begins giving a speech until they all decide to break for lunch. Lemming goes to a phone to report these events to the British Dental Association.

Lemming is soon shown, wearing dentist garbs, with a patient, telling the camera that he knew something was going on. The Big Cheese made two mistakes. One, not recognizing Lemming, Arthur Lemming, Special Investigator, British Dental Association. And second, (spit!) by the time he got back from lunch, he had dentists waiting for them in the broom cupboard before saying his farewell and for the viewer to keep their teeth clean. After what felt like a title scene, an announcer (Idle) says, 'It's a man's life in the British Dental Association.' The Colonel (Chapman) appears and orders the sketch to end.

- This sketch was written by Michael Palin and Terry Jones.
- In the draft script for the episode, this sketch originally came first.
- The photograph of Arthur Lemming was taken at the BBC Television Centre's photographic studios on September 11th, 1969.
Red Indian in Theatre is a sketch that appears in "It's the Arts," the sixth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

An American Indian (Eric Idle) enters a theatre, where the audience is awaiting the performance to begin. He speaks to the man next to him (Graham Chapman) about his tribe's profound interest in theatre arts and his admiration for Cicely Courtneidge.

The house manager announces that Courtneidge will not be appearing and he is killed by arrows.
Science Fiction Sketch is a sketch that appears in "You're No Fun Anymore," the seventh episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The sketch is introduced by a man in a red coat (Michael Palin).

An opening narration (John Cleese) tells the audience of creatures from an alien planet that come to earth to conquer and destroy civilisation. He introduces ordinary couple Mr and Mrs Samuel Brainsample (Graham Chapman, Eric Idle), but quickly shifts the focus to Harold Potter, who is turned into a Scotsman by the creatures from another planet.

- This sketch (and the subsequent connected sketches) were written by Michael Palin and Terry Jones. The ending was partially rewritten by Graham Chapman and John Cleese.
- Much of the sketch was filmed in and around Bradford between September 22 and 26, 1969.
- The New Pudsey railway station was used for the film's opening shots.
- The shot of Harold Potter transforming into a Scotsman was filmed on Southmere Terrace.
- The shot of the man at the bus stop transforming into a Scotsman was filmed near Cragg Street.
- The football sequence was filmed on the Bradford FC ground of Valley Parade.
- The redcoat's introduction was filmed at the children's swimming pool area of Staines Recreation Ground on September 15, 1969.
- The shots of the man having to drive his own bus were filmed on India Way at the junction with Commonwealth Avenue in West London on September 17, 1969.
- The model shots of the flying saucer were filmed in the 'Puppet Theatre' stage at BBC Television Centre on September 17, 1969.
- The shots of the line of Scotsmen heading north was filmed on or around September 23, 1969. Many of the Scotsmen were members of the show's production team to save costs on extras.
Ron Higgins is a professional Cardinal Richelieu impersonator. He is summoned as Richelieu to speak for the defence of Harold Larch, but is exposed as Ron Higgins by Inspector Dim of Scotland Yard.

Ron Obvious is a sketch that appears in "Untitled," the tenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Ron Obvious of Neaps End (Terry Jones) runs along the shore, with hopes of being the first man to jump the English channel. He is interviewed prior to his attempt, noting that his manager, Luigi Vercotti (Michael Palin) told him it would be easier to jump over water than dry land. The interviewer (John Cleese) speaks to the reluctant Vercotti just before Ron's failed cross-channel jump. Vercotti states that Obvious' next attempt at a feat will be the following week, his goal being to eat Chichester Cathedral.

Ron tries to eat the cathedral, but injures his teeth. Ron's next event is to tunnel from Godalming to Java.
Restaurant Abuse/Cannibalism is a sketch that appears in "Intermission," the thirteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A husband Douglas (John Cleese) and wife Shirley (Eric Idle) enters a restaurant lobby, the wife complaining about everything.

They greet the waiter (Terry Jones) who leaves to commit suicide. The head waiter (Michael Palin) informs them that this is a vegetarian restaurant only, who angrily describes disgusting ways animals are killed to be served. He then asks them if they want to know why he still wets his bed.

The head waiter's headmaster (Graham Chapman) enters and greets him. A man dressed in long Greek robes enters and starts to narrate a story before being sent out by the head waiter.

Shirley asks for the menu and as she and Douglas argue, a waiter pulls along a large serving platter with the first waiter sitting half-naked, calmly on it, ready to be cooked. He acknowledges them and tells Douglas and Shirley to "enjoy" him this evening as he's the special. He then points to the vicar (Idle) who is sitting in a pot and tells them not to try him.

Shirley starts to complain about everything again before the same intermission screen from the previous sketch appears, with the voice over saying "There will now be a whopping great intermission" before linking to the next sketch.
School Prize-Giving is a sketch that appears in "It's a Living," the nineteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The bishop of East Anglia (Michael Palin) gives a speech at his old school's prize-giving ceremony before being pulled under the table by a hidden person. A second bishop (Eric Idle) stands and informs the audience that the first man was an imposter wanted by the police. The other assembled dignitaries continue to look and smile, unfazed by the turn of events. He picks up where the first bishop left off, with a silver cup that he promptly stuffs into a sack. He moves on to the Fairfax Atkinson trophy, and claims that no student this year met the required standard in applied mathematics to receive it, so he stuffs it and all the other silver trophies into his sack (due to an 'old rule of school'), before being pulled down by another person.

The first bishop gets up and attempts to pick up where he left off before being pulled down again. Another man (Graham Chapman) speaking in a Chinese accent identifies himself as the bishop and proudly claims the Fyffe-Chumleigh spoon for the People's Republic of China, but is pulled down by yet another person, Inspector Elizabeth Bradshaw (Terry Jones) who starts to present the trophies. Suddenly, he is shot down by machine gun fire.

A soldier appears from behind the table (John Cleese) and two other soldiers crouch down and shoot into the audience. The soldier announces not to panic and tells everyone to get down, as the building is surrounded. He starts awarding the trophies properly over the loud noise of gunfire and the other table members sit oblivious to the surroundings. The first winner, Forbes Minor, is shot down and the soldier starts to award the next prize but the screen freezes and zooms out to reveal it is a TV monitor showing Mr Dibley's film, If.
Raymond Luxury-Yacht Interview is a sketch that appears in "It's a Living," the nineteenth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

An interviewer (Michael Palin) introduces Britain's leading skin specialist Raymond Luxury-Yacht (Graham Chapman). However, Raymond says it isn't his name and it is pronounced "Throatwobbler Mangrove". The interviewer refuses to interview him as he is being silly, and Luxury-Yacht accuses him of anti-semitism. The interviewer pulls his fake nose off and tells him to go away.
Secretary of State Striptease is a sketch that appears in "The Attila the Hun Show," the twentieth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The Compere (Eric Idle) walks on stage of the Peephole Club and introduces the Secretary of State on commonwealth affairs.

The curtains open and the Secretary (Terry Jones) enters, wearing a smart suit and a bowler hat. Jazz music plays as he undresses, garment by garment, and he talks about Commonwealth relationships.

The Compere goes on stage and presents the Minister of Pensions and Social Security (Graham Chapman) who enters, wearing a suit and cropped shirt and tie, bellydancing to Arabic music.
Ratcatcher/Wainscotting is a sketch that appears in "The Attila the Hun Show," the twentieth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The parent from the last sketch (Terry Jones) enters his house, his wife (Michael Palin) sitting on the sofa knitting. They are Mr and Mrs Concrete. Mr Concrete answers the doorbell and the ratcatcher Leslie Ames (Graham Chapman) enters. He tells them that their flat has been chosen as the venue for the third test against the West Indies. When Mrs Concrete asks in delight "Really?" he says it was a joke and he is the council ratcatcher.

Mrs Concrete describes how the rat has been scrabbling down at the wainscotting and the ratcatcher repeats "Wainscotting" wistfully, and says it sounds like a "little Dorset village". It cuts to a village called Wains Cotting and an excited housewife (Eric Idle) runs out of her house and announces to the camera "we've been mentioned on telly!"

The ratcatcher kneels down by the wainscotting and hears sheep bleating. Mrs Concrete finds a mouse hole but the rat catcher pulls out a line of mice and continues looking for another hole. He finds a large hole cut in the wall hidden by an armchair.

Just then, a group of cricketers enter and asks if the third test in here and Mr Concrete sends them out, saying it was a joke. The ratcatcher announces he's going in the wainscotting and the same Wains Cotting lady rushes out of her house and says "they said it again!"

The ratcatcher goes in the hole to lay down some sheep poison but emerges clutching his arm, claiming it's got a gun.
Registrar is a sketch that appears in "Archaeology Today," the twenty-first episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

The Registrar of Marriages (Terry Jones) sits at his desk working. A couple enter (Eric Idle and Barbara Lindley) and the man tells him he was here on Saturday getting married to a blonde girl and he'd like to swap, as the other one wasn't good. The registrar tells him he can't do that. The man asks if he could borrow one for the weekend and the registrar still says no. A referee (John Cleese) enters, blows his whistle, and takes the man aside. He reveals a number 8 on his back, and asks for his name, which is Cook. The actors of the next sketch shrug at the camera and begin.
Scott of the Antarctic is a sketch that appears in "Scott of the Antarctic," the twenty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Chris Conger (Graham Chapman) is in Paignton, Devonshire, where for the next six months, it will be used as a filming location for Scott of the Antarctic. He interviews producer Gerry Schlick (Eric Idle). He asks how they're going to deal with the lack of snow and Schlick explains how they will use Wintrex, a new foam rubber which looks like snow on-screen, and lots of white paint for a "special finish".

Schlick explains actor Kirk Vilb (Michael Palin) is the title role and the director is James McRettin (John Cleese). McRettin greets Conger (in a bad Scottish accent) enthusiastically and is incapable of answering his questions about filming. He eventually manages to explain that the first scene they will shoot is the scene outside the tent.

The scene they will be shooting is where Scott returns to the tent to have brunch with the rest of the team. Cockney officer Terence Lemming (Terry Jones) plays Oates, and Olympic pole-vaulter Seymour Fortescue plays Bowers, both of whom are sitting bored outside a tent.

It cuts to shots of the film and McRettin jumps on screen to say "great!" and cues the next character before running off screen. Vanilla Hoare (Carol Cleveland) as Miss Evans forgets her line and a stagehand runs on to tell her her line, "good morning, Captain Scott." to which she hesitatingly repeats. She tells the director she's not very happy with the line and would like to say "Hi, Scotty" instead. He enthusiastically runs on screen to tell her that's great, and runs off. Vanilla continues to get her line wrong and asks the director if she can say it in a more overexcited way. He agrees. Schlick goes on screen to tell McRettin that Kirk is too tall for Vanilla, and he concludes that Kirk should take his boxes off and Vanilla should get up out of the trench. Vanilla very much disagrees with that and demands she act in the trench. McRettin dismisses everyone for lunch.

Later in the afternoon, Schlick explains they will be shooting the scene where Scott gets off the boat, sees a lion, fights it and kills it. Conger tells him there aren't any lions in the Antarctic and Schlick realises the problem and tells McRettin to lose the lion. Kirk asks why angrily and Schlick carefully explains that there are no lions in the Antarctic. Kirk demands he fight the lion because that's very important, and Schlick suggests he should fight a penguin. McRettin is so excited he falls over. Kirk tells him how the lion is in the contract and Schlick decides that they will somehow use the lion. Conger tells him lions are found in Africa, and Schlick decides to move the story to Africa: Scott of the Sahara.
Scott of the Sahara is a sketch that appears in "Scott of the Antarctic," the twenty-third episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Triumphant music plays over a title card of the movie trailer and the camera moves down to an English seaside, with an expedition team, surrounded by dogs.

A voiceover (Michael Palin) announces productions by the same team who brings Scott of the Sahara: Lawrence of Glareorgan, Bridge Over the River Trent, The Mad Woman of Biggleswade and Krakatoa, East of Leamington.

He describes Lieutenant Scott's encounter with a desert lion. Scott (Palin) rips open his coat and it cuts to stock footage of a lion jumping at him. It then cuts to Scott, having a stuffed lion thrown at him and wrestling with it on the ground, and later, an actor in a lion suit. Shots of the epic fight consist of the lion holding a dagger, Scott stepping on his foot and eventually knocking him out with a punch. The lion neatly spews blood.

The voiceover describes Oates' (Terry Jones) struggle with a giant electric penguin and it cuts to a model penguin robotically turning to face the camera. Royal Hospital for Over-Acting is a sketch that appears in "Spam," the twenty-fifth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

It cuts to the Ypres 1914 sketch again, where they writers have tried to make it less silly. It begins as usually until the Major (Graham Chapman) enters and tells everyone they only have rations for four of them, but there are five. They all suggest they pull a short straw to see who will have to leave the group and they do so, but the Major pulls the short straw. He demands they do it again but he pulls the short straw again. The Major tells them "best of three" and he once again pulls the short straw. In attempt to reverse his fate, he suggests he could put someone up for a posthumous VC but the others don't look so keen. He suggests they do fisties and they all pull out fists, except for the Major who pulls out scissors.

In a last desperate attempt, he says that everyone who doesn't want to stay here raise their arms, and they all do, apart from the padre (John Cleese) who doesn't have any. Padre angrily says an inspirational speech. He's carried off on a stretcher and driven to the Royal Hospital for Over-Acting, still saying his dramatic monologue.

A doctor (Chapman) tells the camera how all the patients are suffering from overacting, surrounded by actors who exaggeratedly act as their character.

He enters the Richard III Ward where four actors are dressed in similar Richard III costumes. One actor evilly mutters the "a horse! A horse!" line. A nurse comes and chloroforms him.

The doctor presents one actor (Eric Idle) who sits on his bed reading calmly. He explains how they operated on him from the Chichester festival just in time.

Rival Documentaries is a sketch that appears in "A Book at Bedtime," the thirty-eighth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A reporter (John Cleese) stands in a field, asking a question regarding the "Spot the Looney" presenter's view that Sir Walter Scott is a loony and starts to document him until another reporter (Michael Palin) asks for his microphone, which he complies, only for him to start a documentary on trees. The first reporter confusedly trails him, until they start fighting for the microphone, talking between the documentaries of Sir Walter Scott and trees. The first reporter has the camera cut to Scott's friend, Angus Tinker (Graham Chapman), who talks about what he had been working on until a forestry expert (Terry Jones) steals the microphone to talk about timber. The first reporter arrives in a car, swiping the microphone, and resumes talking about Scott until the second reporter arrives, and they resume their rivalry about their documentaries until they end up crashing into something.

The 'Book At Bedtime' presenter (Palin) has got to the end, reading 'The End' and the credits roll. Footage of Edward Heath and members of Parliament plays and a 'Spot the Loony' buzzer is heard.
Schoolboys' Life Assurance Company is a sketch that appears in "Mr and Mrs Brian Norris' Ford Popular," the twenty-eighth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

A group of schoolboys, Stebbins, Tidwell and Balderston (Eric Idle, Terry Jones and Terry Gilliam), enter the schoolmaster's office (Michael Palin). The schoolmaster accuses them of running a unit-trust linked assurance scheme with fringe benefits and full cash-in endowment facilities. He tells them to stop this “extra-curricular capitalist expansion”.

The real reason he has called the boys in is to help his wife with her urinary problems, and asks which one is the surgeon. Tidwell admits he is the surgeon but says Stebbins is a gynaecologist. The schoolmaster hires him for 30 guineas to have an examination and report done by break.

Rustic Monologue  is a sketch from "Owl-Stretching Time", the fourth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

Two flunkeys carry a sedan chair onto a beach. A gentleman exits and the flunkeys undress him to reveal a bathing suit. The gentleman stands for a few seconds before running back into the sedan chair. The flunkeys carry it into the sea.

A singer (Eric Idle) is seen in bed, with a women licking and frolicking with him, singing "Jerusalem (And Did Those Feet)". He then introduces a number called "England's Mountains Green".

A farmer (John Cleese) says "Yes, you know, it's a man's life in England's mountains green". The Colonel (Graham Chapman) stops the sketch and threatens if the British Army's slogan is parodied anymore, he'll stop the whole programme, and demands they do a sketch involving teeth. The farmer asks about his rustic monologue as he's "not sleeping with that producer again".

An announcer announces excitement, drama, action, violence, fresh fruit, passion, thrills, spills, romance and adventure as all things you can read about in a book.

Revolting Cocktails is a lost sketch that originally appeared in "E. Henry Thripshaw's Disease", the thirty-sixth episode of "Monty Python's Flying Circus".

At a bar, "The Fox and Half-a-Bee", three city gents enter to find a cheerful bartender (Graham Chapman) at work. They all call him different names and describe their orders. Mark (Terry Jones) requests a special. The bartender suggests a “twist of lemming" to which Mark agrees to have one. The bartender squeezes a lemming's neck into the glass and gives Mark his drink. Alex (Michael Palin) requests a Mallard Fizz. As the city gents have a conversation, the bartender puts some angostura and vodka into a cocktail shaker, beheads a mallard to put its head in and puts an egg and tabasco sauce in as well. He frantically shakes the shaker. After drinking his drink, Mark runs off to vomit as Alex is given his drink.

The final city gent (John Cleese) requests "Harlem Stinger". At which, Rastus (Terry Gilliam), the bartender's assistant, comes in and is given multiple bottles and some extras which he gargles and spits out. Alex drinks his Mallard Fizz and leaves. The city gent pays for the drinks and swallows his Harlem Stinger. He runs to the bathroom door to try and vomit but instead vomits in a waste paper basket. Mark returns pale and asks the bartender to be easy on the lemming next time. Alex comes back and asks for something lighter, eventually settling on a Safari Snowball. The city gent asks if there are any cocktails that aren't horrible to which the bartender replies "I'm afraid not, sir". The city gent ponders why they even come to the bar.
It is unknown why the sketch was cut from the episode but it is presumed to be because of the violent and dark nature of the cocktail's ingredients.
The sketch features on the album Live at Drury Lane, finishing with the bartender suggesting a "dog turd and tonic" for Alex (the latter recoiling at the idea).

Spam is a sketch that appears in "Spam," the twenty-fifth episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus.

In the sketch, two customers are trying to order a breakfast from a menu that includes the processed meat product in almost every dish. It features Terry Jones as The Waitress, Eric Idle as Mr Bun and Graham Chapman as Mrs Bun. The televised skit also featured John Cleese as The Hungarian, but this part was left out of audio recordings of the sketch.

Mr. and Mrs. Bun float down into a café (oddly inhabited by Vikings) and ask what's on the menu. The waitress (Terry Jones) lists off the items:

Mrs. Bun (Graham Chapman) asks if there's anything without spam in it. The waitress and Mr. Bun (Eric Idle) start giving her options for dishes with little spam in them. However, she doesn't want any spam, so she requests a spam dish without the spam. The waitress retches at the thought. The vikings (The Fred Tomlinson Singers) start singing about spam until the waitress silences them. The waitress explains that Bun can't have the spam dish without spam as it wouldn't be a spam dish without. Mr. Bun tells his wife to not make a fuss as he'll just have her spam as he's having spam, spam, spam, spam, spam, spam, baked beans, spam, spam, spam and spam. The waitress says that the baked beans are off so the husband asks if she can replace it with spam. The Vikings start singing again so the waitress silences them.

A Hungarian gentlemen (John Cleese) walks into the restaurant and tries to request a dish off the menu but only ends up complimenting the waitress' breasts and explaining how his lower intestine is full of the dish he is trying to request, due to his faulty phrasebook. He is then hit by the waitress' spoon and bundled off by a police constable.

We then see A Historian (Michael Palin), in a studio, explaining how another great Viking victory was at the Green Midget Café in Bromley. He tries to explain their tactics but ends up chanting "spam". The studio set then is hoisted up, to reveal the café, again, as the historian runs off to join the Vikings' singing. Mr. and Mrs. Bun float out of the café as the screen fades to black.

The credits then roll with the crew members' names having the word "spam" and/or breakfast items inserted into them.

We then cut to Karl Marx (Jones) and Che Guevara (Terry Gilliam) in bed. Karl switches off the light, ending the episode.

It premiered on December 15, 1970 as the final sketch of the 25th episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus, and the following end credits were changed so every member of the crew has either Spam or some other food item from the menu added to their names. Despite its shortness, the sketch became immensely popular. The word "Spam" is uttered at least 132 times.

This sketch has also been featured in several Monty Python videos including Parrot Sketch Not Included - 20 Years of Monty Python.

Spam was one of the few meats excluded from the British food rationing that began in World War II and continued for a number of years after the war, and the British grew heartily tired of it, hence the sketch.

When the Hungarian tries to order food, his words are "My lower intestine is full of Spam, Egg, Spam, Bacon, Spam, Tomatoes, Spam." Yet the subtitles read "Your intestine is full of Sperm."  This is a continuation of the "Dirty Hungarian Phrasebook" sketch, earlier in the episode. The subtitles are a continuation to an argument some Python fans have waged over whether the Hungarian is saying "Spam" (which would be logical) or "Sperm" (which is what it sounds like, and would tie in better with the Hungarian phrasebook's wording).

The song opened the 1982 film Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl, where it was lip-synched by Graham Chapman, John Cleese, Terry Gilliam and Terry Jones dressed as waiters in a performance which, at the suggestion of Python touring member Neil Innes, ended with them revealing their bare backsides. In 2002, a similar rendition was mimed by Eric Idle, Terry Jones, Terry Gilliam and Neil Innes at the Concert for George, a memorial concert for George Harrison which took place at the Royal Albert Hall. At the end of this rendition the four men turned their backs to face a portrait of George Harrison, thereby revealing their naked buttocks and effectively mooning the Albert Hall audience. More recently it was featured as an animated number in A Liar's Autobiography, performed by the London Gay Men's Chorus, both on the recorded soundtrack and live, as a flash mob, during the screening shown during the London Film Festival. The song also opened the second half of Monty Python's 2014 reunion shows where it accompanied a suggestive dance routine by the 20-strong dance ensemble, with Eric Idle and Michael Palin encouraging an audience singalong.

Prior to the album's release, Monty Python received legal threats for alleged copyright infringement due to the similarity between "Sit on My Face" and "Sing as we Go". Nonetheless, the Pythons decided to retain the song.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has ruled that the song is "actionably indecent", concluding that "despite English accent and 'ambient noise' ... the lyrics were sufficiently understandable". In 1992, it pursued legal action against KGB-FM, a San Diego, California classic rock radio station, for playing the song, eventually forcing the station to pay US$9200 in fines.

A French language rendition of the song presented in Edinburgh in 2003 translated the title as "Cum in my Mouth". According to producer Rémy Renoux, "Cum in my Mouth is ... what [Monty Python] would have written today." Renoux also claimed that the translation met with the approval of the Monty Python team.

Monty Python's Spamalot is a comedic musical "lovingly ripped off from" the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975). Like the film, it is a highly irreverent parody of the Arthurian Legend, but it differs from the film in many ways, especially in its parodies of Broadway theatre. Eric Idle, a member of the Monty Python team, wrote the musical's book and lyrics, and collaborated with John Du Prez on the music. Running since March 17, 2005, it was directed by Mike Nichols and won three Tony Awards, including the Tony Award for Best Musical of the 2004–2005 season.

Idle explained the title in a February 2004 press release about the musical:
"I like the title Spamalot a lot. We tested it with audiences on my recent US tour and they liked it as much as I did, which is gratifying. After all, they are the ones who will be paying Broadway prices to see the show. It comes from a line in the movie which goes: ‘we eat ham, and jam and Spam (food) a lot."
